To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) visual attention is controlled by a saliency map that encodes for the conspicuity of stimuli; (ii) the conspicuity of a stimulus critically depends on the visual context; (iii) the saliency map can be used to control attention and eye movements; and (iv) the conspicuity map can be computed from image features such as luminance, color, orientation, and motion, and from the results of object recognition
The perceptual saliencies of visual stimuli critically depend on the surrounding context and that a saliency map is an efficient and plausible mechanism for the bottom up control of attention.
the conspicuity of visual stimuli depends on the context and that the conspicuity is computed by the saliency map.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the computational modelling of visual attention and its neural underpinnings.
the development of computational models of visual attention that are grounded in neurobiological and psychological principles.
developing and testing computational models of visual attention that are grounded in the neurobiological reality of the visual system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the computational models of focal attention have been successful in capturing many of the important features of visual attention.
attention is not just one thing.
the computational modeling of visual attention has come of age.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the visual system is a hierarchical system, where each layer of the hierarchy has a specific task and that each layer is connected to the next layer.
we have shown that it is possible to model the deployment of visual attention with a biologically plausible and computationally efficient model.
the brain uses a bottom-up saliency map for the selection of attended stimuli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not a passive recipient of sensory input, but actively shapes its input by selectively amplifying the information it deems relevant.

attention is an emergent property that results from the interaction between bottom up and top down control processes, and that the computational principles of visual attention are best understood within the framework of a Bayesian decision theory.
the visual system is highly efficient at selecting the most informative locations in the visual environment for further processing.
